newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - U.S. states eager to raise cigarette taxes.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - U.S. states eager to raise cigarette taxes.

text.p: Where there's smoke, there's potential revenue, at least in the eyes of state lawmakers who have unleashed their annual flurry of proposals to raise cigarette taxes.
"I think you are going to see a lot of states talking about this, a lot of states proposing large increases," said Kurt Wenner, policy analyst for the non-profit watchdog group Florida TaxWatch.

Alaska's governor has proposed raising his state's cigarette tax by $1 to $1.29 a packet. New Hampshire's governor is calling for a 25 cents a pack increase; Maryland's wants to double its cigarette tax to 72 cents.

Florida Governor Lawton Chiles, whose state is among those suing tobacco companies to recoup the public cost of treating smoking-related illnesses, proposed a 10 cents a packet rise, while Maine's has proposed doubling its to 74 cents.
A Virginia senator is also seeking a 10 cents a packet increase, spread over four years with a 2.5 cent increases annually.

The rate increase plans coincide with tobacco wars in the courts, which have generated a frenzy of allegations that cigarette makers tinkered with nicotine levels in a deliberate effort to hook consumers on a product they know is harmful.
CIGARETTES VIEWED AS EASY PREY But lawmakers have always
viewed cigarettes as sinful, and therefore easily taxable.

"In any given year, in every legislature there's at least one proposal from some legislator to raise the cigarette tax. Any time you have something with a stigma attached to it, it becomes somewhat easier to tax," said Scott Mackey, a tax analyst for the National Conference of State Legislatures.
"People voting for a tax increase can make the argument that you're doing this as much for the impact on behaviour as to raise the revenue," Mackey said.

"It's an easy target," agreed Peggy Carter, spokeswoman for R.J Reynolds Tobacco Co."When the states need to go looking for additional revenues, it's usually at the top of most legislators' minds. Taxes on tobacco products are among the highest on any consumer product on the market today."

Every state has a cigarette tax, ranging from a modest 2.5 cents a pack in Virginia to a whopping 81.5 cents a pack in Washington state. The median for states is 31 cents and comes on top of the 24 cents a pack levied by the federal government.

Often the revenues go into state general funds. When cigarette tax increases are profferd via citizens' initiative, as happened recently in Massachusettes and Arizona, the new money is more likely to be earmarked for health care or anti-smoking programmes.

No state has ever adopted an increase as large as the $1 a packet hike proposed in Alaska, Mackey said. Increases in the 10 cent range are more the norm. BIG INCREASE CAN BACKFIRESteeper hikes can reduce cigarette sales to a degree, several analysts said. But that can backfire because then the state loses revenue. That is especially true when surrounding states have lower tax rates, said Roy Burry, a tobacco industry analyst for Oppenheimer & Co.
"People just go across the border," Burry said. "There really is no effect whatsoever unless of course it's California. People aren't going to go from Los Angeles to Nevada to buy cigarettes."
Cigarette company profits generally are unaffected by nickel-and-dime tax increases because the hikes are passed on to consumers, Burry said.
The taxes are collected and paid to the states by cigarette wholesalers, who control limited franchise areas that generally do not cross state lines.
"The wholesaler, who's operating at a thin profit margin, has to pass it on," Burry said.

Nor is it likely that smoking can be taxed out of existence, industry officials said. Tobacco products are made and sold in every nation in the world and, no matter what advertising restrictions are adopted or taxes levied, at least 20 percent of adults continue to smoke, Carter said.
"There is going to be a group of people who enjoy smoking enough that they are not going to get that price-sensitive to it," Carter said.

There is no way to predict how many of this year's proposals will survive the legislative process. Typically, Mackey said, cigarette tax hikes fare better when governors throw their weight behind them.
Maryland's governor has raised the ante by making the cigarette tax hike part of a larger package that would reduce income taxes across the board.
"There's a sweetener there," Mackey said.

But previous increases proposed by the Alaska and Florida governors have failed. So did one endorsed last year by some of the tobacco companies themselves. That proposal by the Associated Industries of Florida business lobby was part of a doomed effort to persuade Florida to drop its suit against the cigarette makers.
The lawsuit, which is still pending, could still affect the outcome of Florida's proposed increase.
"If Florida is successful in recouping money from the tobacco companies, I think it would alleviate some of the pressure to increase taxes," Wenner said.
OTHER FACTORS A variety of other factors affect the
outcome of cigarette tax hike bills.
"It really depends on the year, the dynamics, whether the budget is in good shape," Mackey said.

With last year's strong economy, only two states adopted increases, according to National Conference of State Legislatures records. Massachusettes raised its cigarette tax from 51 cents to 76 cents per pack and Utah bumped its up from 26.5 cents to 30.5 cents.
"Last year was a very quiet year for cigarette tax increases," Mackey said.
The general anti-tax mood of the nation could also snuff out many of the proposals, even where lawmakers fervently oppose cigarette smoking.
"A lot of states are saying 'Hold the line.' The legislature's going to be very resistant to any kind of tax increases," Wenner said.
